newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu government now stable, spokesman says.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu government now stable, spokesman says.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu intends to turn to important matters of state now that he has quelled a three-week cabinet crisis, his spokesman said on Tuesday.
"The government is going to act on the really important matters now that this affair has come to an end," said spokesman Shai Bazak. "The coalition is going to be really stable now."
But a PLO official voiced doubts a Middle East peace deadlock could be broken soon.

Analysts added that while Netanyahu had solved one cabinet crisis by strengthening Foreign Minister David Levy's hand in peacemaking, he merely fanned another by snubbing ultra-hawk Ariel Sharon's bid for more power in the government.

Israeli-Palestinian peace talks have been on hold since Netanyahu sent bulldozers in March to break ground for a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem. The PLO demands Netanyahu stop the work before negotiations can resume. He has refused.
Netanyahu on Monday appointed lawyer Yaacov Neeman to the vacant post of finance minister at the expense of Sharon, considered to be a sure bet to win the Treasury.

The prime minister also bowed to Levy's demand to grant him formal control of peace talks with the Palestinians and do away with an inner ministerial forum on key policy issues on which Sharon demanded a seat.

Analysts said a disgruntled Sharon, a champion of Jewish settlements in occupied lands whose potential ascent rattled Arabs and Israel's key ally the United States, would become another thorn in Netanyahu's side.

"Netanyahu succeeded in creating another ominous rival in the form of Mr Sharon," political scientist Ehud Sprinzak told Reuters. "Sharon is a powerful force within Netanyahu's Likud party. This could create serious problems for in the long run."
Sharon, who holds on to his post as national infrastructure minister, praised Neeman's appointment and laughed off reports he felt betrayed.
"Really now, you must be joking," the burly ex-general chortled on army radio.
Netanyahu, tossing Sharon an olive branch, said he would seek his advice on peace moves.

The Israeli leader suffered two key Likud cabinet defections during his first year in office. Right-winger Benny Begin, son of the late Prime Minister Menachem Begin, resigned as science minister in January and Dan Meridor vacated the finance ministry in June.
Netanyahu named loyalist Michael Eitan science minister.

Some analysts backed Bazak's prediction the cabinet changes -- due to be submitted for parliamentary approval on Wednesday after a procedural delay on Tuesday -- could put some life into stalled peace moves with the Palestinians.

"We have now just about turned the corner on the domestic political deadlock. This will mark the start of more serious talks with the Palestinians, where we are still left with more substantive deadlock," said Gerald Steinberg of the Begin-Sadat Centre for Strategic Studies at Bar-Ilan University.

The clock is now ticking towards September, when Israel is due to implement the second of three promised troop withdrawals from West Bank rural areas -- although the Palestinians rejected Israel's first pullback offer as too stingy.
Political analysts were sceptical Netanyahu's new cabinet, more loyalist with the addition of Neeman and Eitan, could meet the September deadline.
"Nothing has changed. They haven't changed their stances and it is built into this government that it responds only to outside pressures," said political scientist Meron Benvenisti.
"It's just time to wait for the next crisis."
Palestinians said Israeli domestic turmoil had frustrated efforts to start talking again but Netanyahu's reshuffle -- and snub of Sharon -- made little difference.
"Sharon's existence in the government at all is a negative factor for any progress in the peace process," Palestinian cabinet secretary Ahman Abdel-Rahman told Reuters.
"The current Israeli government has become a prisoner for the extremist groups."
